historical_timeline.summary: Entered the Augustinian monastery at Erfurt; ordained in 1507.
A disturbed conscience and the spiritual trials he called Anfechtungen.
Severe headache and whizzing in the ear in Bologna.
Professor of the Bible at Wittenberg.
At the Wartburg after the Diet of Worms; painful constipation and sleeplessness.
Regular headaches with fainting spells and vertigo, reported by his physician.
First urinary stone, passed after severe pain.
Severe depression during the disputes over the Lord's Supper.
Broke off a sermon because of severe dizziness.
Attack of roaring tinnitus in the left ear, nausea and collapse; tinnitus persisted afterwards.
Depression returned; plague in Wittenberg, where he stayed to care for the sick.

claims.statement: Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 (Julian calendar) in Eisleben, into a relatively prosperous mining family; his father, Hans, gave him a good education and intended him for law.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The date is in the Julian calendar used in the Empire at the time; it is 19 November 1483 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar.

claims.statement: He entered the University of Erfurt in 1501 and became a Master of Arts in 1505; later in 1505, after a vow to St Anna made in a thunderstorm, he entered the Augustinian monastery at Erfurt against his father's wishes, and he was ordained in 1507.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context.

claims.statement: As a monk, although he made full use of confession, he felt that he was 'a sinner before God with an extremely disturbed conscience', and this anxiety and fear meant that he underwent what he termed Anfechtungen, spiritual trials or temptations, in particular about predestination.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of recurrent spiritual crises; not a diagnosis. Anchors the history of earlier low periods.

claims.statement: He became professor of the Bible at Wittenberg in 1512 and held the post until his death. He published the Ninety-Five Theses on 31 October 1517, refused to recant at the Diet of Worms in 1521, was declared an outlaw, was sheltered at the Wartburg, and returned to Wittenberg on 6 March 1522.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context: his work and the public conflicts of his life.

claims.statement: In 1525 he married Katharina von Bora, a former nun; they had six children, two daughters of whom died young.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context; no health fact, statement or decision of his wife or children is used in the modern episode.

claims.statement: In May 1521, at the Wartburg, he wrote to Philipp Melanchthon that the Lord had afflicted him with painful constipation, and that he had not slept all night.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented constipation, which Feldmann lists among his common, correctly recognized illnesses.

claims.statement: In the autumn of 1510, in Bologna, he reported severe headache and whizzing in the ear; from 1523, according to his physician Matthias Ratzeberger, he had regular headaches with fainting spells and vertigo.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Earlier head and ear symptoms reported in his letters and by his physician, as cited by Evers.

claims.statement: From 1526 on he had sporadic attacks of urinary stones, which reminded him of death because of the excruciating pain; the first stone, in 1526, was preceded by headache, heaviness in the head, vertigo and nausea and was passed through the urethra.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented urinary stone disease before the index date; Feldmann calls them bladder stones. Anchors the stone history and prevention plan.

source_links.locator: 1526: first urinary stone, passed through the urethra

claims.statement: On 22 April 1527 (Julian) a severe attack of dizziness forced him to break off a sermon.
claims.clinical_interpretation: An earlier vertigo attack in the same year.

source_links.locator: April 22: a dizzy spell forced him to stop preaching
22 April 1527: severe vertigo attack interrupted his sermon

claims.statement: On the evening of 6 July 1527 (Julian), when he was 43, he had an attack that began with a roaring tinnitus in his left ear, which increased and seemed to fill the left half of his head, followed by nausea, pallor, coldness and a state of collapse without loss of consciousness; he prayed and believed he would not survive the night. After a night's rest all the symptoms had subsided except the tinnitus, which persisted. His friends Justus Jonas and Johannes Bugenhagen wrote accounts of it.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented attack that anchors the presenting problem.

source_links.locator: Jonas and Bugenhagen; left ear; nausea; following week unable to work
July 6: buzzing in his left ear

claims.statement: In the first half of 1527 he was deeply disturbed by disputes with other reformers over the Lord's Supper and suffered severe depression.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A popular history by a magazine editor; anchors the low mood at presentation. Not a diagnosis.

claims.statement: His depression and illness returned in August, September and late December 1527; he wrote to Melanchthon that he had spent more than a week 'in death and hell'. When plague broke out in Wittenberg in August 1527, he stayed to care for the sick and his house became a hospital.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; history only.

source_links.locator: August, September, and late December; 'death and hell'; plague

claims.statement: Feldmann concluded from Luther's letters and his friends' reports that the attacks with tinnitus and vertigo that began in 1527 were a typical case of Ménière disease of the left ear, more than 330 years before Ménière's description; earlier writers had read them as a psychiatric disorder or as chronic inflammation of the middle ear, and a later Japanese review reads them as chronic suppurative otitis media.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective diagnosis; he was never so diagnosed. Anchors the synthetic modern Ménière disease.

claims.statement: Evers, applying modern criteria to the letters, found that some of his vertigo attacks met the criteria for Ménière disease, that others occurred with headaches meeting the criteria for vestibular migraine, and that his headaches partly met the criteria for migraine; he concluded that vestibular migraine with migraine and Ménière disease is possible but not final.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective differential; supports considering vestibular migraine in the modern episode.

claims.statement: Psychiatric readings of his life are disputed: the Danish psychiatrist Paul Reiter diagnosed him as manic-depressive in a work of 1937 to 1941, while Grossmann in 1956 could not show a consistent link between low mood and reduced drive in 1527 and 1528 and spoke of a cyclothymic personality; a recent review notes that the behavior of a historical person cannot be judged objectively from the sources.
claims.clinical_interpretation: No historical psychiatric diagnosis is adopted; the modern depression is synthetic.

claims.statement: In 1537, at the meeting of the Schmalkaldic League in Schmalkalden, he had his worst attack of stones: he told his wife that not a drop of water had passed from him for days and that he had been as good as dead, and he felt as if born again when his bladder opened.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; history only. The month was not verified in a fetched source.

claims.statement: After 1530 he had headaches, often with ringing or buzzing in the ears, which after 1541 sometimes forced him to stop work and avoid sunlight, and an open sore on his leg, which physicians kept open for drainage from 1543; similar attacks of tinnitus and vertigo recurred irregularly, and from 1528 hearing loss was mentioned.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; history only.

claims.statement: A Norwegian pathologist's review lists among his bodily illnesses varicose ulcer, angina pectoris with anxiety, obesity, hypertension, Ménière disease, constipation with hemorrhoids, urolithiasis, gout and a cataract in one eye.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective list from a short review; used only as history.

claims.statement: On his last journey to Eisleben, from 1 February 1546, to settle a dispute between the counts of Mansfeld, he had chest pressure, breathlessness and weakness of the left arm; after a similar attack he died in Eisleben, the town of his birth, on 18 February 1546 (Julian).
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; history only. Feldmann gives the attack as on the 17th; death on 18 February is used, as the Luther Memorials Foundation and the Stanford Encyclopedia give it.

claims.statement: Feldmann and a Japanese review conclude that he died of a coronary thrombosis (myocardial infarction).
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective cause of death; history only.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognizing and managing Ménière disease in a 43-year-old man with attacks of spinning vertigo, roaring tinnitus and muffled hearing in one ear, under the AAO-HNS 2020 clinical practice guideline and the Bárány Society criteria: a careful history of attack duration and ear symptoms, audiometry to document low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, MRI to exclude a vestibular schwannoma, vestibular migraine and stroke in the differential, salt and caffeine advice, a diuretic as maintenance, the weak evidence for betahistine, limited use of vestibular suppressants, vestibular rehabilitation for chronic imbalance, and intratympanic steroids held in reserve; recurrent depression recognized alongside a frightening chronic illness, with a DSM-5-TR diagnosis, the PHQ-9, a structured safety assessment, CBT and an SSRI by shared decision under the APA 2019 guideline, and the sodium risk of an SSRI with a thiazide; an acute ureteral stone in a man with an earlier stone, with medical expulsive therapy, stone analysis and a 24-hour urine to guide prevention under the AUA guidelines; and preventive care at 43.

assessment_plan.assessment: Colicky flank-to-groin pain, 30 red cells per high-power field and a known stone history fit renal colic. referral.question: Recurrent attacks of spinning vertigo for about three months, lasting hours, with roaring tinnitus, fullness and muffled hearing in the left ear, in a 43-year-old man; the tinnitus persists between attacks. Please confirm the cause, arrange audiometry and any imaging, and advise on preventing attacks and protecting his hearing
referral.pertinent_history: Three attacks in about three months. One forced him to stop speaking in public; the worst, twelve days ago, began with roaring in the left ear that seemed to fill the left side of his head, then spinning, nausea, pallor and collapse without loss of consciousness, settling after a night's sleep except for the tinnitus, which has continued. Headaches on and off for years, and noises in the ears in his twenties. No hearing loss on the right. A urinary stone passed last year. Depression screen positive (PHQ-9 15, item 9 scored 0), being assessed in primary care. Examination today: ear canals and tympanic membranes normal, Weber to the right, no spontaneous nystagmus, normal head impulse test, Dix-Hallpike negative on both sides, normal cranial nerves, coordination and gait. Blood pressure 128/82. Blood count, electrolytes, kidney function, calcium, uric acid and TSH normal. Meclizine 25 mg allowed for severe attacks only. No other medicines; no known allergies

consultant_note.history: Professor Luther, 43, is seen at the request of Dr. Brandt-Mensah. Over about three months he has had three attacks of spinning vertigo, and one more six days ago, each lasting from about one to six hours, with nausea, and each preceded or accompanied by roaring tinnitus and fullness in the left ear and muffled hearing on that side. Between attacks the left-ear tinnitus continues at a lower level. He does not lose consciousness. No attack has come with headache, light or sound sensitivity, or visual aura; he has dull headaches on some other days, without dizziness, and had head and ear noises in his twenties. No ear discharge, ear surgery, head injury or ototoxic drugs. He drinks three to four cups of coffee a day and beer with dinner, and his diet is salty. He is frightened of an attack while preaching or lecturing
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Brandt-Mensah's intake note, examination and tests (blood count, electrolytes, kidney function, calcium, uric acid and TSH normal) and his attack diary. Audiometry today: left low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss of 40 dB at 250 and 500 Hz and 30 dB at 1000 Hz, 15 to 20 dB above that; right ear normal; word recognition 88 percent left and 100 percent right; type A tympanograms on both sides

exam.finding: Ear canals and tympanic membranes normal on microscopy; tuning forks: Weber to the right, Rinne positive on both sides
No spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus with fixation removed; head impulse test normal on both sides; no head-shake nystagmus
Cranial nerves normal, including facial and trigeminal function; coordination normal; gait and Romberg steady

assessment.display: Ménière disease of the left ear, definite
assessment.assessment: He meets the AAO-HNS 2020 and Bárány Society criteria for definite Ménière disease: two or more spontaneous attacks of vertigo each lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, low- to medium-frequency sensorineural hearing loss documented by audiometry in the left ear, and fluctuating tinnitus and fullness in that ear, not better explained by another vestibular diagnosis. The normal examination between attacks argues against a central cause. Vestibular migraine was considered: he has headaches, but no attack has carried migraine features, so the criteria for vestibular migraine are not met; the two can coexist, and a headache diary will show whether that is so. The asymmetric hearing loss calls for MRI to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. Vestibular function testing and electrocochleography are not needed to make the diagnosis

Sodium restriction and limiting caffeine and alcohol are reasonable first steps. A diuretic is a guideline option for maintenance; hydrochlorothiazide also lowers urine calcium, which may help his stones, but his sodium should be checked, particularly if an SSRI is started. Betahistine is not FDA approved in the United States and the large BEMED trial found it no better than placebo, so it is not recommended. Vestibular suppressants such as meclizine should be limited to attacks, because regular use slows compensation

Hearing is fluctuating and word recognition is still good; no hearing aid is needed now. If unsteadiness persists between attacks, vestibular rehabilitation helps; it is not useful during an attack. If disabling attacks continue after about three months of these measures, an intratympanic steroid injection is the next step; gentamicin or surgery are reserved for refractory disease

recommendations: Sodium 1,500 to 2,300 mg a day, caffeine to about one cup a day, and alcohol limited; keep the attack and headache diary
Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg each morning, with sodium and potassium in two to four weeks
Meclizine only for severe attacks, for no more than three days at a time; sit or lie down at the first warning
MRI of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium
Vestibular rehabilitation if unsteadiness persists between attacks
Repeat audiogram at about three months, and sooner with any change in hearing
Intratympanic steroid if disabling attacks continue after about three months
Depression care to continue with Dr. Brandt-Mensah; the attacks and the fear of them feed the low mood
